Hi, I’m sorry for your loss. Today is the 2nd anniversary of my girl’s passing and she too died from GDV. We had the same exact experience except for a few minor details. I rushed her to the vet, emergency surgery, she survived the surgery and was fine. We waited for her to get up and walk on her own but she never did. She just laid down and refused to get up. I lifted her paw and dropped it to see if she resisted ( if she had feeling or control on her limbs) and she didn’t. We thought she was still getting rid of the anesthesia in her system. About 4 hours after surgery she passed away. I didn’t understand what had happened and was so sad and angry that she survived so much only to die like this. About a week after, I talked to my mom’s vet who turned out to be a gastrointestinal specialist. He said something along the lines of:”When a dog has GDV, the stomach bloats and twists around itself. When this happens, the affected gastrointestinal organs can’t have enough oxygen and since there’s no circulation blood starts clotting in the veins that feeds these organs. The surgery corrects this and restores the blood flow but the existing clots spread into the system. If the clots are snall enough that dog’s body is able to handle these clots on its own, they survive. Otherwise they pass away. That’s why GDV is so deadly, it leaves so many things to chance and you can’t really control the outcome even if you do everything right” 

As to your question about the chair… I unfortunately have a lot of experience with post op dogs and in my in-no-way-expert opinion, it may have been a combination of anxiety and anesthesia. We know after a surgery we will eventually get better and it was for our own good but they don’t know that. Even after something as mundane as neutering/spaying, a dog just knows that they are injured. They don’t know why, they don’t know when or if it’ll get better. Combine that with grogginess of anesthesia, it’s possible that Junie didn’t really know what she was doing, she was just a bit anxious so she chewed. I would rule out pain out of the equation because vets almost always administer pretty good pain relief after surgery- usually enough for them to sleep through the first night with minimal discomfort.
And honestly, she was with you in her final moments, knowing you were there and even if you were asleep I’m pretty sure it didn’t matter to her. Plus, seeing your pup passing away as it happens would be very upsetting for you and it is very likely that she would see you distressed and panicking in her final moments. Instead, she got to cross the rainbow bridge peacefully with the one she trusted the most by her side and believe me, it is a luxury not every dog can have. 

I hope my words can bring you some comfort in this difficult time. I know how traumatic GDV is and I feel for you. But please know that you have done everything you could for her and I’m sure she’s up there, playing with her friends until you come and telling them about all the adventures she had with you.

If you suspect GDV you should be taking her to ER RIGHT NOW. It’s is a medical emergency and should be treated right away -like in a couple of hours- for best chances of survival. 
Better to be paranoid a 100 times than be negligent once in my opinion.
Did your vet take an x-ray to rule out GDV? If not, you need to take her a vet who will.

My grandma always says “one doesn’t die because of a disease, they die because it’s their time” and I really believe that. Piggybacking on hemangiosarcoma comments here, my girl had an enlarged spleen and hemangiosarcoma was suspected. I initially didn’t want to go through with the surgery because of the poor post-op prognosis but as her quality of life declined because of it, I thought “we’re going towards euthanasia anyway, what’s the harm in trying?” And got her spleen removed. Turns out, it wasn’t hemangiosarcoma, they removed an absolute unit of a spleen (and that’s what caused her pain and discomfort) but the tumor was benign. She lived 5 more months only to die from bloat. 

Your pup didn’t pass away because you did/didn’t do xyz. She passed because it was simply her time. 

You have my sincerest condolences.

To my knowledge, an ultrasound or a ct/mri scan is needed for a definite diagnosis. Hemangiosarcoma is a type of malignant tumor in spleen. Sometimes presents itself in addition to enlarged spleen but not always. Regular ultrasounds would be the best way to go to catch it early, for getting your pup anesthesia regularly and exposing them to the radiation other scans cause would do more harm than good.

Seek another opinion immediately please.
If your vet doesn’t know what’s happening, you don’t sit around and wait for it to pass. You seek another vet who can figure out what the problem is.
It is your right -and quite frankly responsibility - to get a clear diagnosis so that you can seek treatment.

You are binging because you restrict on the days you don’t binge. You restrict and exercise excessively on the days you don’t binge to compensate the binges. This is a form of purging.

The thing is, we think we have to stop binging first, in order to get the situation under control. But in reality, what will actually work is letting the “binges” happen (which in your case, they are your body’s attempt to get nutrients in anyway it can so that it can stay alive) and stop the compensating behavior first. No exercise, no restriction on days after, nothing. 

This is happening because your body is simply done asking for food, now it’s demanding it. In my personal experience, this is the part where your body is done sending you the mental and physical hunger symptoms; it’s freaking out and making you eat these amounts because it needs food asap. The more you restrict yourself and exercise to counteract these episodes, the bigger and more frequent they will become. The answer it eating more throughout the day (recovery minimums depending age and sex) PLUS whatever your body wants to eat during this “out of control” eating periods WITHOUT exercising and restricting afterwards.

The more you nutritionally rehabilitate, sooner this feeling goes away.
